h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר י״ג Parshas Zachor — Maamar Yud Gimmel

p: for it includes all the matters
that stand against the kelipah of Amalek.
For the essence of his kelipah
At first, when the time came
and wished to nullify the receiving of the Torah.
"and he cut down among you," etc.,
and it is stated in Midrash Tanchuma (Teitzei 10)
that he would cut off their milos, etc.:
(שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה ל, יב; תַּנְחוּמָא מִשְׁפָּטִים ה)
regarding Akilas, to whom Hadrian said,
"Learn their Torah but do not circumcise yourself,"
וְאָמַר לוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לִלְמוֹד תּוֹרָתָן
and he said to him, "One cannot learn their Torah
to one who is circumcised, etc."
That is, if he circumcises but does not convert,
for he is in the category of the uncircumcised
And this is why he came to accuse
to give the Torah to Yisrael
and he said that they too blemish it —
But his accusation did not avail,
and they received the Written Torah.
דְּשָׁם עִיקַּר מְקוֹם תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
for there is the principal place of Torah she'b'al peh,
"For from Tziyon shall go forth Torah,
and the word of Hashem from Yerushalayim";
"the word of Hashem — this is halachah"
and the Chamber of Hewn Stone —
"from there Torah goes forth to all Yisrael"
(בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה יט, כ; תַּנְחוּמָא חֻקַּת יח)
וּמִי הָיָה מֶלֶךְ עֲרָד זֶה עֲמָלֵק וְכוּלֵּי
"And who was the king of Arad? This is Amalek," etc.
That is, he came to accuse,
לְבַטֵּל מֵהֶם אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
to nullify from them the light of Torah she'b'al peh.
For Amalek is the evil inclination,
as we said (in the previous maamarim)
and he knew that when Yisrael receive the Torah
וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
Likewise afterwards, through Torah she'b'al peh,
they would be able to merit, as at the Giving of the Torah,
לִהְיוֹת חֵירוּת מִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת וְיֵצֶר הָרָע
freedom from the Angel of Death and the evil inclination;
therefore he wished to hold them back.
So too the accusation of Haman, of his offspring,
likewise came when the time arrived
for the spread of Torah she'b'al peh
through the Men of the Great Assembly,
"Many decrees have I decreed upon myself
beyond what You decreed upon me."
as it is written (Daniel 1:8), "And Daniel resolved
that he would not defile himself
with the king's food or with the wine he drank" —
that is, the decree against their wine and their oil
and their daughters too are a decree
We have already said that Haman's accusation,
"and their laws differ from every people" —
that they do not eat of ours
and do not marry of ours
was intended as an accusation above,
לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל גְּזֵירָה זוֹ
before Hashem Yisbarach, about this decree:
that their intent is not for the sake of Heaven
but out of arrogance and hatred of people.
וְאֶת דָּתֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ אֵינָם עוֹשִׂים [אֶסְתֵּר ג, ח]
"and the king's laws they do not keep" (Esther 3:8);
and wherever "the king" is said unspecified,
it serves for both sacred and profane
(אֶסְתֵּר רַבָּה ג, י עַל פָּסוּק גַּם וַשְׁתִּי)
that is, their intention is not
לְקַיֵּים דָּתֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים בָּזֶה
to fulfill thereby the laws of the King of kings
(as explained in Tetzaveh, end of Maamar 2).
So too the accusation "they are asleep regarding the mitzvos,"
and, according to the Rabbis, "they are one people" —
in all of it his intention was
וּמִן הַסְּתָם הָיָה קְצָת מְקוֹם קִטְרוּג
And presumably there was some ground for the accusation,
since he brought about the sealing of
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה [אֶסְתֵּר רַבָּה ז, יג].
as they said in the Midrash Rabbah (Esther Rabbah 7:13).
and carried out the obliteration of Amalek,
כְּתִיב [אֶסְתֵּר ח, טז] לַיְּהוּדִים הָיְתָה אוֹרָה
it is written (Esther 8:16), "For the Jews there was light,"
וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר [מִשְׁלֵי ו, כג] וְתוֹרָה אוֹר
and so it says (Mishlei 6:23), 'and Torah is light'" —
which is called orah, in the feminine form,
for it receives from the Written Torah,
"They accepted it anew in the days of Achashverosh" —
regarding which there was the overturning of the mountain upon them like a barrel;
דְּעַל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב אָמְרוּ נַעֲשֶׂה וְנִשְׁמָע
for about the Written Torah they said, "We will do and we will hear,"
the opposite of the kelipah of Amalek, the evil inclination,
דִּכְתִיב [תְּהִלִּים צז, יא] וּלְיִשְׁרֵי לֵב שִׂמְחָה
as it is written (Tehillim 97:11), 'and for the upright of heart, gladness'";
that is, when the heart is made upright,
and empties all the evil from the heart of the fool,
and becomes one heart to his Father in Heaven.
Amalek is the root of the serpent and the evil inclination,
and it is the opposite of joy;
and when his kelipah is nullified completely and entirely,
this certainly stands against the kelipah of Amalek,
וְקִטְרֵג עַל קְדוּשַּׁת הַבְּרִית שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
and accused regarding the holiness of Yisrael's covenant,
"Yekar — this is the tefillin of the head" (Megillah, ibid.),
which indicates that Yisrael are bound to the root,
beyond the grasp of human intellect.
in saying "the tefillin that are in the head"
and not "that are on the head,"
for the intent is that they are bound in the head, in the mind,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר הָרַב זֵכֶר צַדִּיק וְקָדוֹשׁ לִבְרָכָה.
as the Rav, of saintly and holy memory, said.
and since they merited to carry out the obliteration of Amalek,
they merited the level of yekar,
which indicates attachment to the root,
which comes from the Dew of Atika,
(מִדְרָשׁ חֻקַּת רַבָּה יט, ו; תַּנְחוּמָא ח)
וְכָל יְקָר רָאֲתָה עֵינוֹ [אִיּוֹב כח, י]
"'And his eye beheld every precious thing' (Iyov 28:10) —
this is Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues."
against receiving the Written Torah was nullified,
and Yisrael merited to receive the Torah;
but the accusation against the receiving
and spread of Torah she'b'al peh,
in the hearts of the Sages of Yisrael —
עַל זֶה יֵשׁ קִטְרוּג תָּמִיד מִקְּלִיפַּת הָמָן
against this there is constant accusation from the kelipah of Haman.
מִלְחָמָה לַה׳ בַּעֲמָלֵק מִדּוֹר דּוֹר [שְׁמוֹת יז, טז]
"Hashem has a war against Amalek from generation to generation" (Shemos 17:16),
carry out the obliteration of Amalek anew.
We read before it, on Shabbos,
to put remembering before the doing
דִּמְחִיַּית עֲמָלֵק (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מְגִילָּה ל, א)
of the obliteration of Amalek (as stated in Megillah 30a):
and we merit the obliteration of Amalek
on the part of Hashem Yisbarach on Purim,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ [תַּנְחוּמָא כִּי תֵצֵא ד]
as they said in the Midrash (Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 4):
"And I erase his name from above," etc.
וּבְכָל שַׁבָּת יֵשׁ מְחִיַּית עֲמָלֵק לִשְׁעָתוֹ
And every Shabbos there is an obliteration of Amalek for its time,
וְעַל כֵּן אוֹמְרִים בְּמוֹצָאֵי שַׁבָּת קֹדֶשׁ
Therefore we say on Motzaei Shabbos Kodesh,
so may it be for us":
we ask that the obliteration of Amalek be forever,
we be saved from the accusation of Amalek,
and that we merit the light of Torah she'b'al peh

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 65b, Beshalach — “Rabbi Shimon said that the accusation was against the Holy One above, and below too it was against Him: They took men, cut away the sacred sign, lifted it and threw it upward, saying, ‘Take what You desired.’ The whole confrontation was directed against the Holy One.” The mockery attacks the sign of the covenant. The Zohar calls this a confrontation directed against the Holy One both above and below.

paragraphs.text: Tanchuma, Mishpatim 5; Shemos Rabbah 30:12 — “Hadrian said: You should have learned Torah without becoming circumcised. Akylas answered: Have you ever given a soldier his allowance unless he took his weapon? So too, if a person is not circumcised, he cannot learn Torah, as it says, ‘He declares His words to Yaakov’—to one circumcised like Yaakov. ‘He has not done so for any nation,’ because they are uncircumcised.” Shemos Rabbah 30:12 preserves the same exchange and Akylas’s praise of the truth of Israel’s Torah. Rav Tzadok uses the dialogue to explain why Amalek targeted the covenant before the giving of Torah.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 31b — “If one vows, ‘I may not benefit from the uncircumcised,’ he may benefit from uncircumcised Israelites but may not benefit from circumcised members of the nations. If he vows, ‘I may not benefit from the circumcised,’ he may not benefit from uncircumcised Israelites but may benefit from circumcised members of the nations. For uncircumcision is used as the designation of the nations, as it says, ‘All the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised of heart.’” The Mishnah is interpreting the communal language of a vow. Rav Tzadok draws from it the distinction between the physical operation alone and entry into Israel’s covenant.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 138b — “‘The word of Hashem’—this is halachah. ‘The word of Hashem’—this is the end of exile. ‘The word of Hashem’—this is prophecy.” The sugya interprets the hunger to hear Hashem’s word in Amos 8. Rav Tzadok takes its first identification, halachah, when reading “the word of Hashem from Jerusalem.”

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 86b — “If they have not heard a ruling, both groups come to the Great Court in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, from which Torah goes forth to all Israel, as it says, ‘From that place which Hashem will choose.’ If the elder returns to his city and teaches as he formerly taught, he is exempt; if he instructs people to act, he is liable. He is not liable until he instructs them to act.” The Mishnah locates final public legal authority in the Temple court. That concrete institution supplies the maamar’s association between Jerusalem and the unfolding of Oral Torah.

paragraphs.text: Tanchuma, Chukas 18; Bamidbar Rabbah 19:20 — “When Aharon died, the clouds of glory departed and Israel appeared like a woman whose hair was uncovered. Who was the king of Arad? This was Amalek, as it says, ‘Amalek dwells in the land of the south.’ He sat at the breach. When he heard that Aharon had died and the clouds of glory had departed, he immediately attacked them.” Bamidbar Rabbah 19:20 gives the same identification and explains why Scripture calls him a Canaanite. Rav Tzadok places this renewed attack at the threshold of Eretz Yisrael and the Oral Torah.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 21b — “‘New as well as old, my beloved, I have stored away for you’: The congregation of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the world, I have imposed many decrees upon myself beyond what You decreed upon me, and I have fulfilled them.” The additional decrees are presented as Israel’s loving offering. The maamar contrasts that motive with Haman’s accusation that separation comes from pride or hatred.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 36a — “Rav said: Scripture says, ‘Daniel resolved in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s food and the wine of his drinkings.’ It speaks of two drinkings: wine and oil. Rav held that he resolved in his own heart and instructed all Israel; Shmuel held that he resolved in his heart but did not instruct all Israel. The Gemara then explains Rav’s account: Daniel decreed against oil in the city, and the later Sages extended the decree even to the field.” The source distinguishes Daniel’s initiating restriction from the broader enactment attributed to the students of Hillel and Shammai. Rav Tzadok focuses on the emergence of these protective practices.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 36b — “They decreed against their bread and oil because of their wine; against their wine because of their daughters; and against their daughters because of another matter. But is the prohibition concerning their daughters not biblical, ‘You shall not intermarry with them’? The biblical prohibition concerns the seven nations; the Sages came and extended the decree to the other nations.” The Gemara describes safeguards against intermarriage and idolatry. On 36a Rav derives a decree from Daniel’s abstention, while Shmuel reads it as personal resolve. The maamar follows the tradition assigning Daniel an initiating role.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 13b — “‘Their laws differ from every people’: They do not eat of ours; they do not marry our women, nor give their women in marriage to us. ‘They do not observe the king’s laws’: They pass the year with their excuses and holidays. ‘It is not worthwhile for the king to leave them’: They eat and drink and disparage the king. Even if a fly falls into one of their cups, he throws it out and drinks; but if my lord the king touches the cup, he dashes it to the ground and will not drink.” These are the malicious allegations attributed to Haman. Rav Tzadok reads the earthly accusation as also challenging the intention behind Israel’s safeguards, not as the Gemara’s own judgment about their motive.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Divrei Soferim 32 — “In the days of Achashverosh, though ‘they accepted it anew with love,’ it was not through revelation of Godliness but from within concealment and darkness.” Rav Tzadok there defines the “orah” of Purim: Torah she’b’al peh, the light that shines in darkness, as in “He set me in dark places — this is the Talmud of Bavel.” This is why Purim will never be annulled.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 41 — “With tefillin in particular, one should annul and include the wisdom and understanding of his divine soul within the wisdom and understanding of the Infinite One, blessed be He, clothed particularly in the passages ‘Sanctify’ and ‘When He will bring you.’ He should use his soul’s wisdom and understanding for Hashem alone. So too, he should annul and include his soul’s knowledge, embracing the love and fear in his heart, within the supernal Knowledge clothed in ‘Hear’ and ‘If you will listen’—as stated in Shulchan Aruch, to subject the heart and the mind.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Tanya spells out the inward service signified by tefillin: the intellect and heart themselves enter divine service. This clarifies Rav Tzadok’s distinction between tefillin merely resting on the head and an attachment that reaches into the mind. It is a parallel to that idea, rather than an identification of the unnamed teacher quoted in the maamar.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, Kedushas Levi, Derush lePurim, s.v. Od yevo'ar: shalchah lahem Esther — “Oral Torah varies according to the sages of the generations: one says one thing and another says another, and the conduct of halachah follows the generations. … In truth Israel loved to receive Torah, saying, ‘We will do and we will hear’; but initially they did not wish to receive Oral Torah. … They found it difficult that Oral Torah should vary according to the will of the righteous sage of each generation, who draws down the attribute through which the world is governed. This is why the Sages said, ‘They accepted it again in the days of Achashverosh’: through love of the miracle they accepted this too. Mordechai and Esther brought about that acceptance.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Kedushas Levi locates the difficulty of accepting Oral Torah specifically in its continuing realization through the sages of successive generations. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok says the accusation against Oral Torah must be overcome afresh: acceptance embraces living Torah authority as it continues to unfold, beyond a single historical giving of Torah. Kedushas Levi explains this through changing divine attributes, a formulation distinct from Rav Tzadok’s present account of accusation.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 30a — “Rav says to advance the reading, so that performance should not precede remembrance. Shmuel says to postpone it: Since the walled cities perform Purim on the fifteenth, performance and remembrance occur together.” The discussion concerns Purim falling on Friday and the scheduling of Parshas Zachor. Rav Tzadok adopts Rav’s ordering of remembrance before the act of Purim.

rich.text: Megillah 30a

— “Rav says to advance the reading, so that performance should not precede remembrance. Shmuel says to postpone it: Since the walled cities perform Purim on the fifteenth, performance and remembrance occur together.” The discussion concerns Purim falling on Friday and the scheduling of Parshas Zachor. Rav Tzadok adopts Rav’s ordering of remembrance before the act of Purim.

paragraphs.text: Havdalah, introductory verses — “‘The Jews had light, joy, gladness and honor.’ So may it be for us. ‘I shall lift the cup of salvations and call upon the name of Hashem.’” The addition “So may it be for us” turns the verse into a prayer at the passage from Shabbos into the working week. Rav Tzadok explains that prayer through the continuing removal of Amalek’s inner accusation.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Ki Sisa 9 — “At the third meal Yisrael attain rest from the evil inclination’s accusation… therefore every Motzaei Shabbos before Havdalah we say ‘The Jews had light’… for that erasure was only for its time.” Rav Tzadok there links the custom to Shabbos as “the day Hashem gives you rest,” when “Yaakov and his sons rest.” That rest is the condition the pasuk sets for erasing Amalek.
